script.opening: "I’ve had this chest pain for a few days and I’m really scared it’s my heart — I keep googling heart attacks. But it’s a sharp pain on the left, and honestly it hurts more when I press on it or take a deep breath. I’m 32 — could it still be serious?"

facts.text: Four days. Sharp, in one spot on the left of the breastbone. Worse pressing on it (can press on camera and say "Yes, that’s it exactly"), deep breaths, twisting, lying on that side. Not brought on by walking or stairs. Lasts a while, eases with paracetamol.
If asked: started the gym a week ago — lots of press-ups and a new chest-press machine. Had a cold with a cough the week before.

No heaviness or tightness, no spread to arm, jaw or back. No sweating, no breathlessness, no palpitations, no fainting. No calf pain or swelling, no coughing blood, no recent surgery, flights or immobility. Not on the pill (uses the copper coil). No fever. No heartburn or pain with food.

If asked: went to the urgent treatment centre on day 2. "They did a heart tracing — they said it was normal — and my blood pressure and oxygen were fine. The doctor pressed on my chest and said it was sore there."
Well. No medicines, no allergies. Non-smoker. Cholesterol never checked. Her uncle had a heart attack at 50 last month — that’s what set off the panic (only if asked about family or worries).
Works as a solicitor; very stressed at work. Lives with her husband.

Anxious, talking quickly, wants proper reassurance — "Tell me it isn’t my heart. Properly." Simple reassurance without explanation won’t settle you. Calms if the doctor explains why it isn’t the heart. Ask: "And the googling?"

ice.ideas: "I know it hurts when I press, but I keep reading that heart attacks can be different in women."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her uncle’s heart attack last month; she is checking her pulse many times a day and can’t sleep.
ice.expectations: "Tell me it isn’t my heart. Properly."

checkpoints.text: Takes chest pain SERIOUSLY and EXCLUDES serious causes first — cardiac (ACS/angina), PE, pneumothorax, pneumonia, GORD, aortic — via history, risk factors and the recorded examination and observations (PERC/Wells for PE, NICE NG158), with an ECG where any doubt and emergency referral if ACS is suspected (NICE CG95)

Makes a POSITIVE diagnosis of COSTOCHONDRITIS (localised anterior pain reproducible on palpation of the costochondral junctions, worse on movement/breathing) — while recognising reproducible tenderness alone does not fully exclude cardiac disease, and distinguishing Tietze’s syndrome (swelling)

Manages with reassurance, explanation, analgesia (topical NSAID/paracetamol; oral NSAID only after checking asthma, GI, renal, cardiovascular risk and pregnancy) and self-care, avoiding over-investigation once the serious is excluded
Addresses the cardiac FEAR/health anxiety with GENUINE, grounded reassurance (landing because the serious was taken seriously/excluded) — not dismissiveness

Acts where there is any doubt/atypical or risk features (emergency referral for suspected ACS without delaying for tests, NICE CG95; Wells/PERC and D-dimer pathway for PE, NICE NG158; CXR if lung disease suspected) rather than falsely reassuring
Explores and supportively addresses recurrent health anxiety, and checks understanding
Checks what she understands and believes about her heart, corrects misconceptions in plain language, and agrees a clear plan including when to seek help so she leaves reassured rather than dismissed

Safety-nets clearly: red flags warranting urgent/999 care (central/crushing/exertional pain, breathlessness, radiation, sweating, collapse, pain unlike this), and review — positive diagnosis after exclusion, not dismissal

worked.txt: "You were right to come — chest pain always deserves to be taken seriously, even at 32. Let me check the important things first so any reassurance I give you actually means something."

"Is the pain ever brought on by exertion, central or crushing, spreading to your arm or jaw, with sweating or breathlessness? … No. Any calf swelling, sudden breathlessness, coughing blood, recent surgery or long journey, previous clots or the pill? … No. The urgent treatment centre checked your pulse, blood pressure, oxygen, chest and legs, and your heart tracing was normal. Could you press beside your breastbone for me — is that the pain?"

"Now — the pain is sharp, in one spot, worse when you breathe deeply, and — here’s the telling bit — I can reproduce it by pressing on the ribcage. That points to costochondritis: inflammation of the rib-cartilage joints. It’s harmless and settles."
"So I can reassure you genuinely — not by brushing it off, but because I’ve checked your heart and the serious causes. This is muscular/joint pain, not your heart."

"An anti-inflammatory gel on the sore spot, or paracetamol, is a good start — if you need tablets like ibuprofen, I’ll check they’re safe for you first (asthma, stomach, kidneys, pregnancy). Heat, and easing off aggravating movements, help; it usually settles over a few weeks."

"But do seek urgent help — 999 — if you ever get central, crushing or exertional chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, pain spreading to your arm/jaw, or anything different from this. And if the worry keeps troubling you, come back — we can help with that too."

f.learning: COSTOCHONDRITIS is musculoskeletal chest-wall pain — sharp, LOCALISED anterior pain, worse on movement/deep breathing/palpation and REPRODUCIBLE on palpation of the costochondral junctions — but it should be a POSITIVE diagnosis made after taking chest pain seriously and EXCLUDING the serious causes: cardiac (ACS/angina — central/heavy/exertional pain, radiation, sweating, breathlessness, risk factors), PE (pleuritic, breathless, calf, risk factors), pneumothorax, pneumonia, GORD, pericarditis and aortic causes, assessing history/risk factors (PE: two-level Wells and PERC per NICE NG158), using a recorded or in-person examination, and doing an ECG where any doubt — while suspected acute coronary syndrome means emergency referral without delaying transfer for tests (NICE CG95; a normal resting ECG does not exclude ACS). Visible swelling of a single junction suggests Tietze’s syndrome. Crucially, reproducible chest-wall tenderness alone does NOT fully exclude cardiac disease, so the absence of red flags and an appropriate assessment matter, and any doubt or atypical/risk features warrant investigation rather than false reassurance. Manage costochondritis with reassurance and clear explanation, analgesia (topical NSAID or paracetamol; an oral NSAID at the lowest dose for the shortest time only after checking asthma, GI, renal, cardiovascular risk and pregnancy — BNF), heat and activity modification, reassuring that it is self-limiting over weeks and avoiding over-investigation once the serious is excluded. The communication core is the patient’s cardiac FEAR/health anxiety (often google-fuelled): address it with genuine, grounded reassurance — which lands precisely because the serious has been taken seriously and excluded — rather than a dismissive "it’s nothing", exploring and supportively addressing recurrent health anxiety (NICE CG113). Safety-net clearly for red flags warranting urgent/999 care (central/crushing/exertional pain, breathlessness, radiation, sweating, collapse, or pain unlike this).

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG95 (recent-onset chest pain of suspected cardiac origin, 2010, updated 2016) · [2] NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, 2020, updated 2023) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2015 (high-dose ibuprofen) · [4] NICE CG113 (generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder, 2011)
knowledge.summary: Costochondritis is a positive diagnosis: sharp, localised anterior chest pain, worse on movement and deep breathing, reproduced by pressing on the costochondral junctions. It is made only after the history, risk factors and examination (recorded observations, ECG, and self-palpation on video) have made cardiac, thromboembolic and respiratory causes unlikely. Chest-wall tenderness makes a cardiac cause less likely but does not exclude it. When the assessment is reassuring, say so clearly and explain why, offer simple analgesia and safety-net for red flags.

points.t: Ask about central, heavy or tight pain, pain on exertion, radiation to the arm, neck or jaw, sweating, nausea, breathlessness and collapse. Consider acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia, pericarditis, aortic dissection and reflux. If acute coronary syndrome is suspected, follow NICE CG95 [1]: refer as an emergency if pain is current or recent, and do not delay transfer for tests.

Pleuritic pain can be PE. NICE NG158 [2] uses the two-level Wells score, and where clinical suspicion is low the PERC rule. PERC is negative only if all apply: age under 50, heart rate under 100, oxygen saturation 95% or more, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no previous DVT or PE, no unilateral leg swelling, and no surgery or trauma needing hospital treatment in the past 4 weeks.

Costochondritis causes sharp, localised pain at the front of the chest, usually over the second to fifth costochondral junctions, worse on pressing, moving the arms or twisting, and on deep breathing. There is no swelling; visible swelling of a single junction suggests Tietze’s syndrome. Reproducing the exact pain on palpation supports the diagnosis only when the rest of the assessment is reassuring.

Tests are not needed when the assessment is clearly reassuring. An ECG can help if there is any doubt, or to support reassurance, but a normal resting ECG does not exclude acute coronary syndrome (NICE CG95 [1]). Chest X-ray if pneumothorax, pneumonia or other lung disease is suspected.

Explain the cause and that it usually settles over weeks, sometimes longer. Offer a topical NSAID, paracetamol or an oral NSAID at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, after checking for asthma, gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular contraindications and pregnancy (BNF [3]). Doses as per BNF. Heat and avoiding aggravating movements help.

Reassurance works when it follows a visible, thorough assessment and addresses her specific fear. If worry about her health is persistent or causes distress, assess for generalised anxiety or panic and offer support in line with NICE CG113 [4].

model.text: Hello Ms Nair, I’m Dr Clarke. What’s been happening?

I’ve had this chest pain for a few days and I’m really scared it’s my heart. I keep googling heart attacks. But it’s a sharp pain on the left, and it hurts more when I press on it or take a deep breath. I’m 32. Could it still be serious?

You were right to get in touch. Chest pain always deserves to be taken seriously. I’ll ask some important questions and go through the checks and the heart tracing done at the urgent treatment centre, so that whatever I tell you at the end is based on a proper check. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates and explains that reassurance will be earned

model.text: Yes, please.
Can you point to where it hurts, and describe the pain?
Here, on the left of my breastbone. It’s sharp, in one spot.
Does it come on when you walk quickly or climb stairs, and ease with rest?
No, exercise doesn’t change it. Moving and breathing in do.
Does it spread to your arm, neck, jaw or back? Any sweating, feeling sick or faint with it?
No, none of that.
Any breathlessness, coughing up blood, fever or cough?
No.
Any recent operation, long journey, leg swelling, previous clots, or hormone medicines such as the pill?
model.why: PE risk factors including PERC items

model.text: No, none of those.
Do you smoke, and has anyone in the family had heart problems young?
Not that I know of.
Any heartburn, or pain related to eating?
No.
You mentioned reading about heart attacks. What have you been most afraid of?
That I’m having one and nobody’s noticed. Every time it twinges I panic.
That sounds exhausting. What were you hoping I’d do today?
Tell me it isn’t my heart. Properly.

The urgent treatment centre’s checks two days ago are in your notes: pulse, blood pressure, oxygen level, temperature, chest and legs, plus the heart tracing. I’ll go through them, and then I’d like you to press gently on your chest wall for me on the camera.
model.why: Recorded examination and ECG; self-palpation on video

model.text: Okay.

Your pulse, blood pressure and oxygen were normal, your chest was clear, your calves were soft and the heart tracing was normal. Now, if you press with two fingers just beside your breastbone where it hurts — is that exactly your pain?
model.why: Reports reassuring findings and tests reproducibility

model.text: Yes, that’s it exactly.

Then I can explain what I think this is. The pain is sharp, in one spot, worse on breathing and moving, and I can bring it on by pressing where your ribs join the breastbone. With none of the warning signs of a heart problem or a clot, this is costochondritis: irritation of those rib joints. It’s not dangerous and it settles.
model.why: Positive diagnosis explained with the reasoning

model.text: I’m not saying this because you’re young. I’m saying it because the pain doesn’t behave like heart pain, you have none of the danger signs, and your checks and heart tracing are normal. Does that make sense?
model.why: Grounded reassurance tied to her fear

model.text: Yes. It helps to hear why.

For the pain, an anti-inflammatory gel on the sore spot is a good start, or paracetamol. If you need tablets like ibuprofen, I’ll check they’re safe for you first. Warmth helps, and try to avoid movements that set it off. It usually settles over a few weeks.
And the googling?
It’s very understandable, but it tends to feed the worry. If you notice the worry keeps coming back even after reassurance, come and talk to me. There’s good help for that.
Okay, I’ll try.

Call 999 if you get pain that’s central, heavy or crushing, spreads to your arm or jaw, comes with sweating, breathlessness or fainting, or feels different from this. Come back if it isn’t settling in a few weeks. Can you tell me what you’ll look out for?
Heavy or spreading pain, sweating, breathless or faint, or anything different: 999. Otherwise gel and give it a few weeks.
Exactly.

social.t: Searching symptoms can amplify fear. Acknowledge it, and suggest reliable NHS information instead.
Most people can work normally. If lifting or repetitive arm movement aggravates it, discuss adjustments; self-certification covers the first seven days off.

legal.t: Record the negative red-flag features, examination findings, ECG result and safety-net advice. Clear notes protect the patient and the clinician if symptoms change.

professional.t: Tests done only to reassure can increase anxiety if they give borderline results. Explain what a test can and cannot show before ordering it (GMC Good medical practice; decision making and consent).

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) if health anxiety persists.

management.reflectIce: “You were afraid a heart attack was being missed. I’ve checked for that properly, and this pain is coming from your chest wall.”
management.psychosocial: Name the health anxiety kindly; offer support if it persists.
sharedPlan: Topical NSAID or paracetamol; oral NSAID only if suitable, dose per BNF

Return if not settling over a few weeks
safetyNet: 999 for central, heavy or spreading pain, sweating, breathlessness or collapse

pitfalls.intro: Reassurance is the prize in this station, but it only counts if it is earned by a visible, thorough exclusion of the serious causes.

items.why: Serious causes occur at 32, and she will not believe it.
items.fix: Take a focused cardiac, PE and respiratory history and use the recorded findings.

items.why: Tenderness does not exclude a cardiac cause.
items.fix: Combine it with a negative red-flag history and normal recorded findings.

legal.t: Record the negative red-flag features, examination findings, ECG result and safety-net advice. Clear notes protect the patient and the clinician if symptoms change.

professional.t: Tests done only to reassure can increase anxiety if they give borderline results. Explain what a test can and cannot show before ordering it (GMC Good medical practice; decision making and consent).

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) if health anxiety persists.

redFlags: Central, heavy or exertional pain, radiation, sweating or collapse: cardiac
Breathlessness, haemoptysis or PE risk factors: consider PE (NICE NG158)
Tearing pain to the back: aortic dissection
psychosocial: Intense fear of a heart attack

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Costochondritis: sharp, localised anterior chest-wall pain reproduced on palpation of the costochondral junctions, pleuritic and positional, with no cardiac, thromboembolic or respiratory red flags and normal recorded findings.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The joints where your ribs meet your breastbone are irritated. That’s why pressing and deep breaths hurt. It isn’t your heart and it settles.”

management.reflectIce: “You were afraid a heart attack was being missed. I’ve checked for that properly, and this pain is coming from your chest wall.”
management.psychosocial: Name the health anxiety kindly; offer support if it persists.
sharedPlan: Topical NSAID or paracetamol; oral NSAID only if suitable, dose per BNF
ECG to support reassurance where helpful
Return if not settling over a few weeks
safetyNet: 999 for central, heavy or spreading pain, sweating, breathlessness or collapse
Any change in the pain: seek help

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Reassurance is the prize in this station, but it only counts if it is earned by a visible, thorough exclusion of the serious causes.

items.why: Serious causes occur at 32, and she will not believe it.
items.fix: Take a focused cardiac, PE and respiratory history and use the recorded findings.

items.why: Tenderness does not exclude a cardiac cause.
items.fix: Combine it with a negative red-flag history and normal recorded findings.
Ask about PERC items and use NICE NG158.

items.fail: Prescribing an oral NSAID without checks.
items.why: Asthma, GI, renal risks and pregnancy matter.
items.fix: Start with topical NSAID or paracetamol; check before tablets.

items.why: It dismisses her pain and fear.
items.fix: Name the diagnosis and explain the reasoning.

items.why: She needs to know exactly when to call 999.
items.fix: List the features and check understanding.
